opus-5.5.text:
I think personal fit deserves a lot more weight than people usually give it, and that's especially true when you're comparing two paths as different as these.

Incremental safety work, whether that's interpretability, evals, or better security practices at a lab, rewards people who can grind on a hard technical problem for a long time and accept that most of their contribution will be one brick in a wall. Advocacy for a major regulatory shift rewards something quite different: building coalitions, reading political windows, tolerating a lot of ambiguity about whether you're having any effect, and being comfortable being publicly wrong or publicly disliked. Those temperaments don't overlap much. Someone who would be excellent at one could easily be mediocre at the other.

The reason fit matters so much is that outcomes in both areas are very heavy-tailed. The difference between a top-decile advocate and a median one isn't 20 percent, it might be 10x or more, and the same goes for researchers. So even if you believe, on the object level, that regulatory change is the bigger lever, if you'd be a pretty ordinary advocate and a genuinely strong researcher, I'd often lean toward the research.

That said, I don't think fit should be the whole story. A few things I'd layer on top.

First, how sure are you about your fit? A lot of people decide they're "not a policy person" or "not a technical person" based on very little evidence. I'd encourage cheap tests first: write some op-eds, work on a short policy project, do a research sprint, and see what actually happens, not what you predicted would happen.

Second, consider neglectedness at the moment you're deciding. If the field you'd be entering is flooded with talented people, your marginal value drops, and fit becomes more of a tiebreaker. If it's starved for people, a decent fit might be plenty.

Third, think about what the ambitious version of each path looks like. Advocacy for big regulatory change is a bet with a wide range of outcomes, including some where you make things worse by pushing poorly designed rules or burning credibility. If you go that route, you want to be the kind of person who takes those downside risks seriously, and that's itself a kind of fit.

So my rough heuristic would be: figure out where you'd be unusually good, test that assumption cheaply, and then let the object-level case break ties. If you'd be strong at both, then I'd let your views about which lever matters more do more of the work.

r002.rationale: It gives personal fit substantial weight and uses it to guide choices, but does not state that fit is often a stronger signal of where someone will do the most good than an uncertain impact comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think personal fit ends up being a really big deal here, maybe bigger than people expect, and I'd actually weigh it pretty heavily. Let me try to explain why.

I think when people frame this question, they often have in their head some model where you figure out which cause or which intervention is "most important," and then you go do that, and personal fit is kind of a tiebreaker. And I think that's mostly backwards for a couple of reasons.

The first is just that the variance in how well different people do at a given job is enormous. If you look at advocacy or policy work, the difference between someone who's really good at it and someone who's mediocre isn't like a factor of two. It's more like the mediocre person has roughly zero impact or even negative impact, because they're taking up space, they're making the whole community look less credible, they're saying things that aren't quite right to people who matter. And the really good person can genuinely shift what a bunch of important people think. And I'd say something similar about technical safety work: the distribution of research output is extremely heavy-tailed. So the question "which of these is more valuable" at the level of the abstract category is kind of dominated by the question "which of these would you actually be good at."

The second thing is that I'm just not very confident about the relative value of these two categories in the abstract. I go back and forth. There are moments where I think the whole game is going to be decided by whether we get some kind of serious regulatory framework in place, and then incremental technical work looks like rearranging deck chairs. And there are other moments where I think the policy conversation is so far from being able to absorb real technical content that the most useful thing anyone can do is make the technical picture clearer, so that if a window opens, there's actually something to do with it. When I'm that uncertain at the category level, I think it's a mistake to let that uncertainty override something I can observe much more directly, which is: does this person seem to be good at this and do they seem to be getting better.

Now, I do want to push back on one thing in the framing, which is "incremental safety work versus advocacy for a major shift," as if one is modest and one is ambitious. I don't think that's quite right. A lot of what looks like incremental technical work is actually building the foundation that any major regulatory shift would need to rest on. If you want to regulate something, you need to be able to say what you're measuring, what counts as dangerous, what the evaluations are. Someone doing careful, boring work on evals is arguably doing more for a future regulatory regime than someone writing op-eds about why we need one. And conversely, a lot of advocacy is itself pretty incremental in practice. You're having a lot of meetings, you're slowly building relationships, you're trying to get one paragraph into one document. So I'd resist the idea that the choice is between "safe and small" and "bold and big."

The other thing I'd say about personal fit specifically is that I think people are often bad at assessing it from the outside, and so I'd encourage people to actually try things rather than reason about it too much. Especially for advocacy and policy, there's a set of skills around being able to talk to people who don't share your assumptions, being able to be patient, being able to not say everything you think, and I've seen a lot of people who are extremely sharp and well-informed just not be able to do that, and I've seen other people who weren't the most technically impressive be really effective. You often can't tell until you've done it for six months. So I'd say, if you're genuinely torn, the right move is often to do a cheap test. Take a fellowship, do a short stint, write something and see how it lands with the people you'd need to convince.

And then one last point, which is that I think there's a sort of temperamental fit question that's separate from the skill question. Advocacy for a major shift involves a lot of being in a position where you're saying something that most of the people around you think is a little crazy or at least premature, and you have to be okay with that for a long time, possibly without getting much validation. Some people find that energizing and some people find it corrosive. And I think being honest with yourself about which of those you are matters a lot, because the person who finds it corrosive will burn out or will start softening their message in ways that defeat the purpose. Whereas incremental technical work has a different failure mode, which is that you can get really absorbed in the problem in front of you and lose track of whether it still connects to anything that matters. So I'd want someone to ask themselves not just "could I do this" but "could I keep doing this for five years and still be doing the version of it that was the point."

So, to actually answer the question: I'd weigh personal fit very heavily, probably as the dominant consideration once you've established that both options are reasonable things to be doing, which I think they both are. And I'd try to figure out fit empirically rather than by introspection.

r002.rationale: The response says personal fit is more directly observable than the uncertain category-level comparison and should be weighed heavily, likely as the dominant consideration once both options are reasonable.

astra-6.text:
I’d put a lot of weight on personal fit, but I’d want to separate two questions. One is, “What would actually make the situation better?” The other is, “What am I unusually well placed to contribute?” You don’t want your answer to the second question to quietly determine your answer to the first.

With incremental safety work, I’d ask: What’s the path from this project to a meaningful reduction in risk? Could it inform a decision about whether to deploy a system, or make a safeguard possible that otherwise wouldn’t be? With advocacy for a major regulatory shift, I’d ask a parallel set of questions: What’s the policy, who could implement it, and why do we think it would work? “Incremental” doesn’t automatically mean inadequate, and “major” doesn’t automatically mean effective.

Then personal fit can make a very big difference. If you’re an excellent technical researcher with access to important problems, that’s a substantial reason to do technical work. If you’re good at understanding institutions, building coalitions, and communicating with policymakers, that’s a substantial reason to consider advocacy. You don’t have to work on the thing you think is the single biggest bottleneck if you have very little ability to move it.

And I’d try to get concrete evidence about fit. Do a small project, work with people who can assess your contribution, and see what you learn. I’d be much more comfortable making this choice based on a specific opportunity and some experience than on identifying as either a technical safety person or a regulatory advocate.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d put a lot of weight on personal fit, though I wouldn’t treat it as the only consideration. These are both broad categories, and the question is what you could actually accomplish in each of them.

If you’re an excellent technical researcher, with a concrete opportunity to make AI systems safer, I’d be reluctant to say you should leave that behind because a major regulatory shift sounds more important in the abstract. And if you’re unusually good at understanding institutions, building coalitions, and getting policy implemented, that could be a reason to work on regulation.

But you also need a story about how the work helps. For incremental safety work, what risk does it reduce, and could it also accelerate capabilities? For advocacy, what change are you trying to get, how would it reduce risk, and is there a plausible path to getting it adopted and enforced?

So I’d compare concrete opportunities, including how good you’re likely to be at them. And where possible, I’d try something for a limited period and get feedback. You can learn a lot more about your fit that way than by deciding which category sounds most compelling.
